title: Introduction to Anthropology
summary: Discover anthropology: its four fields, ethnography and fieldwork ethics, kinship and marriage, exchange and gifts, ritual and belief, and human origins and ancient civilisations in Africa.
audience: Social-science students, researchers, development workers and curious learners

body.p: Anthropology is the study of humanity in all its diversity, past and present. It asks what it means to be human, how people live in different societies and how humans evolved. Its distinctive approach is holistic (looking at how parts of life connect) and comparative (learning from many societies).

list: Cultural or social anthropology: how people live, think and organise societies today.
Biological anthropology: human evolution, genetics, health and variation.
Archaeology: past societies through material remains such as tools, buildings and food remains.
Linguistic anthropology: language in social life and culture.

body.p: Early anthropology was entangled with colonialism, sometimes producing studies that served colonial administration or portrayed African societies as unchanging. Later anthropologists, including many African scholars, criticised this and emphasised history, change, agency and the voices of the people studied. Today anthropology is used in health, development, business, technology and policy.

body.tip: Practise "making the familiar strange": describe a routine in your community as if seeing it for the first time.

body.p: Anthropologists are known for ethnography: long-term, in-depth study of a community, usually involving living among the people studied. The classic method is participant observation: taking part in daily life while observing and recording.

list: Participant observation and detailed field notes.
Open-ended interviews and life histories.
Genealogies and kinship charts.
Mapping, photography and collecting documents.
Learning the local language to understand meanings from the inside.

body.p: An emic perspective describes things as insiders understand them; an etic perspective uses outside analytical categories. Good ethnography moves between both: understanding what a ritual means to participants and how it compares with practices elsewhere.

Anthropologists must obtain informed consent, protect participants' identities when needed, avoid harm, be honest about their purposes, and share results with communities. Power differences between researchers and participants require reflexivity: awareness of how the researcher's own position shapes the research.

body.tip: Keep a field diary of your own reactions alongside your observations; it helps you notice your assumptions.

body.p: Kinship is the system of social relationships based on descent and marriage. It shapes inheritance, residence, obligations, identity and political alliances.

list: Patrilineal descent traces belonging through the father's line, common in many societies in East and Southern Africa.
Matrilineal descent traces belonging through the mother's line; the Akan of Ghana and the Bemba of Zambia are well-known examples. Inheritance may pass from a man to his sister's son.
Bilateral (cognatic) descent traces through both parents, common in many European societies.
Lineages and clans are larger descent groups, sometimes tracing descent from a common ancestor.

body.p: Marriage creates alliances between families, not only couples. Practices include bridewealth (such as lobola in Southern Africa), where the groom's family gives gifts to the bride's family, symbolising the union of families. Forms include monogamy and polygyny. Kinship terms show how relatives are grouped: in many societies, a father's brother is also called "father", reflecting shared responsibility.

body.tip: Draw your own kinship chart for three generations; notice which relatives you call by the same terms.

body.p: Economic anthropology studies how people produce, distribute and consume goods, and the social meanings involved.

list: Reciprocity: exchange between equals; generalised reciprocity (sharing without counting, within families), balanced reciprocity (gifts expected to be returned), negative reciprocity (trying to get something for nothing).
Redistribution: goods flow to a centre (a chief, a government) and are given out again, such as through feasts or taxes and services.
Market exchange: buying and selling based on prices.

body.p: Marcel Mauss's The Gift showed that gifts create obligations to give, receive and return, building relationships. Bronisław Malinowski's study of the Kula ring in the Trobriand Islands showed how ceremonial exchanges of shell valuables built status and alliances.

Anthropologists study informal markets, rotating savings groups, mobile money, migrant remittances and the social obligations that shape spending, such as funeral contributions, showing that economic decisions are always embedded in relationships.

body.tip: Notice the gifts and obligations in your own community during weddings and funerals; they reveal social ties.

body.p: Anthropologists study religion and ritual as part of social life, describing them respectfully without judging their truth.

Arnold van Gennep described rites of passage marking life transitions such as birth, initiation, marriage and death in three phases: separation from the old status, a liminal (in-between) phase, and incorporation into the new status. Victor Turner explored the liminal phase, where initiates often share a strong bond, called communitas.

list: Rituals use symbols (colours, objects, words, gestures) that carry layered meanings.
Clifford Geertz described culture as "webs of significance" to be interpreted.
E. E. Evans-Pritchard's study of the Azande of Central Africa showed that beliefs about witchcraft formed a coherent system for explaining misfortune.
Religion can provide meaning, community, moral rules and ways to cope with uncertainty.

body.tip: When observing a ritual, ask participants what each part means to them before offering your own interpretation.

body.p: Biological anthropology and archaeology show that Africa is the cradle of humankind. Fossils and genetics trace human evolution over millions of years on the continent.

list: "Lucy" (Australopithecus afarensis), found in Ethiopia, lived about 3.2 million years ago and walked upright.
The Laetoli footprints in Tanzania, about 3.6 million years old, preserve evidence of early bipedal walking.
Sites such as Olduvai Gorge (Tanzania) and the Cradle of Humankind (South Africa) yielded many early human fossils and stone tools.
Fossils from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco suggest that Homo sapiens had emerged in Africa by about 300 000 years ago.
Genetic evidence shows that all living humans descend from African populations, and that Africa holds the greatest human genetic diversity.

body.p: Archaeology reveals ancient African civilisations and trade networks: Egypt, Nubia and Kush, Aksum, the Nok culture of Nigeria, Great Zimbabwe, the cities of the Swahili coast and Mapungubwe. These sites challenge colonial-era claims that Africa had no history.

body.tip: Visit a local museum or heritage site; archaeology is often closer than you think.
